# Setup and reproducibility {#sec-setup}

A tutorial is only useful if you can run it and get the same numbers. This
chapter explains how the project is organised, how to install exactly the
software versions used to build the book, and how Quarto's *freeze* feature
keeps the published book in sync with the code.

## What you need

| Component | Used for | Version used for this book |
|---|---|---|
| R | all analyses | 4.4.3 |
| Bioconductor | DESeq2, recount3, fgsea and others | 3.20 |
| Quarto | building the book | 1.4 or newer |
| renv | restoring R package versions | 1.3.1 |
| conda / mamba (optional) | command-line tools for chapters 4 and 8 | see `envs/ngs.yml` |

About 1.5 GB of disk space is needed for downloads, almost all of it for the
coverage files used in the sashimi plots of @sec-cryptic. Everything else is
small: recount3 gene counts for this study are a few megabytes, and the
junction counts about 25 MB.

## Getting the project

```bash
git clone https://github.com/elmasnuryilmaz/rnaseq-splicing-tutorial.git
cd rnaseq-splicing-tutorial
```

The project layout:

```
_quarto.yml          book configuration (chapters, freeze, bibliography)
index.qmd ...        one .qmd file per chapter
R/helpers.R          shared settings, thresholds and download helpers
R/sashimi.R          sashimi-style plot used in chapter 7
scripts/             shell, Python and R scripts that build the demo BAM files
data/demo/           small outputs of the demo (strandedness, rMATS)
results/             result tables written by the chapters
renv.lock            exact R package versions
envs/                conda environment files
_freeze/             stored results of every executed chapter
data-cache/          downloads (created on first run, not in git)
```

## R packages with renv

[renv](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/) records the exact version of every
R package in `renv.lock`. To install the same versions into a private
project library:

```r
install.packages("renv")
renv::restore()
```

Run this from the project folder. When R starts in the project folder,
`.Rprofile` activates the project library automatically. Bioconductor
packages are restored from the Bioconductor release recorded in the lockfile.

::: {.callout-note}
## How this book was built
The book was rendered in a conda environment (`envs/r-conda.yml`, R 4.4 and
Bioconductor 3.20 packages from conda-forge and Bioconda), and `renv.lock`
was written from that library with `renv::snapshot()`. Both routes give the
same package versions; use whichever fits your system.
:::

## Command-line tools

Chapters [-@sec-strand] and [-@sec-rmats] use HISAT2, samtools, RSeQC,
featureCounts, sra-tools and rMATS-turbo to build and analyse a small demo
data set. Their results are stored in `data/demo/`, so you can read and
render those chapters without installing anything. To rebuild the demo:

```bash
mamba env create -f envs/ngs.yml
mamba activate rnaseq-tutorial-ngs
RSCRIPT=$(which Rscript) bash scripts/make_demo_data.sh
```

`RSCRIPT` must point to an R installation with the project's packages
(step 3 of the script uses rtracklayer).

## Rendering the book, and what "freeze" does

```bash
quarto render
```

The project uses `freeze: auto` (see `_quarto.yml`). When a chapter is
executed, Quarto stores its results (printed output and figures) in
`_freeze/`, which is committed to git. On later renders:

- a chapter whose source has **not** changed is not executed again; its
  stored results are reused;
- a chapter whose source **has** changed is executed again.

This is what lets the GitHub Actions workflow publish the book without
installing R or downloading any data: it only turns the frozen results into
HTML. To force one chapter to run again, render it on its own, for example
`quarto render 05-differential-expression.qmd`. When you render a single
file, Quarto always executes it.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Frozen results can go stale
Freeze only watches the `.qmd` file. If you change `R/helpers.R` or a file
in `results/`, the chapters that use them are not re-run automatically.
Re-render those chapters yourself, in order, before committing.
:::

## Habits that make an analysis reproducible

- **Fix the analysis plan first.** Contrast, model, filters and thresholds
  live in `R/helpers.R` and are set before looking at results.
- **Record versions.** Of the genome, the annotation and every package.
  @sec-report shows how they end up in the Methods.
- **Set seeds** for anything random (`set.seed()` before fgsea and svaseq).
- **Record where and when data were downloaded.** The data inventory in
  @sec-design does this.
- **Keep raw downloads out of git** (`data-cache/` is ignored) but keep small
  results and frozen outputs in it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding
1. You changed a threshold in `R/helpers.R` and ran `quarto render`. Which
   chapters were updated?
2. Why is `_freeze/` committed to git while `data-cache/` is not?
3. What is the difference between `renv.lock` and `envs/ngs.yml`?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answers
1. None. Freeze tracks only the `.qmd` files, so the chapters that use the
   threshold must be re-rendered individually.
2. `_freeze/` holds small, final outputs needed to publish the book without
   re-running the analysis. `data-cache/` holds large raw downloads that can
   be recreated from public sources at any time.
3. `renv.lock` pins R packages; `envs/ngs.yml` pins the command-line tools
   (aligner, counters, rMATS) used outside R.
:::
:::
